solutions.method: Distinguish the group of interest from how much of it is observed.

steps.explanation: The population is the complete set of people or items about which information is required.
A census collects information from every member of that population.
A sample is a selected subset of the population whose observations are used to investigate the population.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Distinguish the group of interest from how much of it is observed.

  1. The population is the complete set of people or items about which information is required.

  2. A census collects information from every member of that population.

  3. A sample is a selected subset of the population whose observations are used to investigate the population.

solutions.method: Separate one selectable member from the list used to select members.

steps.explanation: A sampling unit is an individual member or item of the population that may be selected.
A sampling frame is the list of all the sampling units from which a sample is selected, often numbered.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Separate one selectable member from the list used to select members.

  1. A sampling unit is an individual member or item of the population that may be selected.

  2. A sampling frame is the list of all the sampling units from which a sample is selected, often numbered.

solutions.method: Compare coverage, cost and representativeness.

steps.explanation: A census includes the entire population, removing sampling variability. However, collecting every response can be expensive and time-consuming. It is also unsuitable for destructive tests. A census can still contain measurement or non-response errors.
A sample is usually quicker and cheaper, and creates less data to process. Its disadvantage is that it may not represent the population accurately.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Compare coverage, cost and representativeness.

  1. A census includes the entire population, removing sampling variability. However, collecting every response can be expensive and time-consuming. It is also unsuitable for destructive tests. A census can still contain measurement or non-response errors.

  2. A sample is usually quicker and cheaper, and creates less data to process. Its disadvantage is that it may not represent the population accurately.

solutions.method: Apply the cost and coverage trade-off to 713 club members.

steps.explanation: A census would take time because all 713 members must be contacted and their replies processed, so sampling is reasonable. Alternatively, a census is defensible if the club can easily contact every member and wants complete coverage.
Take a representative sample of members; fewer replies make collection and analysis quicker and cheaper.

  2. Take a representative sample of members; fewer replies make collection and analysis quicker and cheaper.

solutions.method: The test damages the product and the sample is very small.

steps.explanation: Squashing all the loaves would damage all the stock, leaving none suitable to sell.
Two successes out of four gives a sample proportion of 1/2, but four loaves may not represent the whole bakery; the population proportion need not be 1/2.
Test a larger, randomly selected sample drawn across the relevant batches.

solutions.method: Identify the population, individual units and frame coverage.

steps.explanation: Contacting every resident would be expensive and time-consuming.
Each individual resident of the town is a sampling unit.
The register omits residents who are not registered or not eligible to vote, so it does not cover every resident.

  2. Each individual resident of the town is a sampling unit.

  3. The register omits residents who are not registered or not eligible to vote, so it does not cover every resident.

solutions.method: Testing to failure destroys the bulbs; use the data cautiously.

steps.explanation: A census would burn out every bulb, leaving none to sell.

1. The sample mean is close to, and above, 800 hours, so it is consistent with an average-lifetime claim. It does not support a guarantee for every bulb: one lasted only 762 hours.

  2. Increase the number of randomly selected bulbs to reduce the uncertainty from such a small sample.

solutions.method: Random selection must avoid duplicate units.

steps.explanation: In a simple random sample of size n, every possible subset of n population members has the same chance of selection.
Number the 100 units 1–100. Generate random integers uniformly in this range, rejecting repeats, until 20 distinct units have been selected.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Random selection must avoid duplicate units.

  1. In a simple random sample of size n, every possible subset of n population members has the same chance of selection.

  2. Number the 100 units 1–100. Generate random integers uniformly in this range, rejecting repeats, until 20 distinct units have been selected.

solutions.method: Use a random start followed by a fixed interval.

steps.explanation: Systematic sampling selects units at regular intervals from an ordered sampling frame, starting at a randomly chosen position.
Choose a random integer r from 1–5, then select r, r+5, …, r+95. This gives exactly 20 units.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Use a random start followed by a fixed interval.

  1. Systematic sampling selects units at regular intervals from an ordered sampling frame, starting at a randomly chosen position.

  2. Choose a random integer r from 1–5, then select r, r+5, …, r+95. This gives exactly 20 units.

solutions.method: Allocate the sample in proportion to group sizes, then sample randomly within each group.

steps.explanation: Divide the population into non-overlapping strata and randomly sample from each in proportion to its population size.
Choose eight distinct males and twelve distinct females by random numbers from the respective lists.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Allocate the sample in proportion to group sizes, then sample randomly within each group.

  1. Divide the population into non-overlapping strata and randomly sample from each in proportion to its population size.

  2. Choose eight distinct males and twelve distinct females by random numbers from the respective lists.

solutions.method: Use the existing identifiers, but ensure the sex proportions are represented.

steps.explanation: Simple random sampling is straightforward with unique IDs, and gives each member an equal chance of selection.
It may select boys and girls in proportions unlike 75:125.
Randomly choose 15 different boys and 25 different girls from separate lists.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Use the existing identifiers, but ensure the sex proportions are represented.

  1. Simple random sampling is straightforward with unique IDs, and gives each member an equal chance of selection.

  2. It may select boys and girls in proportions unlike 75:125.

  3. Randomly choose 15 different boys and 25 different girls from separate lists.

solutions.method: The interval is 20, so every selected employee number has the same final digit.

steps.explanation: Order the 700 employee numbers. Choose r randomly from 1–20 and select positions r, r+20, …, r+680.

If the list is in consecutive employee-number order, the interval repeats the same final digit. A start ending in 0 can select only managers, whereas other starts omit managers, producing an unrepresentative sample.

The interval is 20, so every selected employee number has the same final digit.

  1. Order the 700 employee numbers. Choose r randomly from 1–20 and select positions r, r+20, …, r+680.

  2. If the list is in consecutive employee-number order, the interval repeats the same final digit. A start ending in 0 can select only managers, whereas other starts omit managers, producing an unrepresentative sample.

solutions.method: A large school contains important subgroups.

steps.explanation: Number the 1,200 students and choose 50 distinct random integers from 1–1,200. A simple random sample may misrepresent the proportions in different year groups.

Use stratified sampling by year group (and, if relevant, sex). Allocate approximately nⱼ students to each group, adjusting integer allocations to total 50, and choose each group’s students randomly without repeats.

solutions.solutionHtml:
A large school contains important subgroups.

  1. Number the 1,200 students and choose 50 distinct random integers from 1–1,200. A simple random sample may misrepresent the proportions in different year groups.

  2. Use stratified sampling by year group (and, if relevant, sex). Allocate approximately nⱼ students to each group, adjusting integer allocations to total 50, and choose each group’s students randomly without repeats.

solutions.method: Opportunity sampling uses accessible people rather than random selection.

steps.explanation: Choose the first available people who are willing to participate.
Stand on the high street and interview the first 20 available shoppers who agree to answer.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Opportunity sampling uses accessible people rather than random selection.

  1. Choose the first available people who are willing to participate.

  2. Stand on the high street and interview the first 20 available shoppers who agree to answer.

solutions.method: Quotas fix group totals but selection within groups is non-random.

steps.explanation: Divide the target population into relevant groups and recruit available people until the required number in every group has been reached.
For example, use known proportions of cinema-goers in age groups to set quotas totalling 30. Approach cinema-goers, assign them to their age group and continue until each quota is full.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Quotas fix group totals but selection within groups is non-random.

  1. Divide the target population into relevant groups and recruit available people until the required number in every group has been reached.

  2. For example, use known proportions of cinema-goers in age groups to set quotas totalling 30. Approach cinema-goers, assign them to their age group and continue until each quota is full.

solutions.method: Explain both accessibility and its possible bias.

steps.explanation: Ask the first five players available. Alternatively, taking the first five on the supplied list is a convenient non-random selection.
The first five on a height-ordered list would be the shortest or tallest, rather than a representative cross-section. The first five available may also differ from the rest.
Use simple random sampling: number every player on the list and choose five distinct random numbers from the full range.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Explain both accessibility and its possible bias.

  1. Ask the first five players available. Alternatively, taking the first five on the supplied list is a convenient non-random selection.

  2. The first five on a height-ordered list would be the shortest or tallest, rather than a representative cross-section. The first five available may also differ from the rest.

  3. Use simple random sampling: number every player on the list and choose five distinct random numbers from the full range.

solutions.method: Identify the selection method and why it may be unrepresentative.

steps.explanation: This is opportunity sampling. Four people is a very small sample, and Tuesday cinema-goers may have television habits unlike the rest of the village.
Increase the sample size and collect responses at different times, days and locations throughout the village.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Identify the selection method and why it may be unrepresentative.

  1. This is opportunity sampling. Four people is a very small sample, and Tuesday cinema-goers may have television habits unlike the rest of the village.

  2. Increase the sample size and collect responses at different times, days and locations throughout the village.

solutions.method: Use the population proportions and check that observations concern the intended population.

steps.explanation: Set quotas of 30 male and 40 female resident drivers. Approach available eligible drivers until both quotas are filled.
Stratified sampling selects randomly within each group; quota sampling selects available people non-randomly until the quotas are full.
Quota sampling does not require a complete sampling frame and can be quicker to organise.
An entering driver may be a visitor, and the car may be borrowed or hired rather than owned by that driver. The observations therefore do not reliably measure cars owned by residents.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Use the population proportions and check that observations concern the intended population.

  1. Set quotas of 30 male and 40 female resident drivers. Approach available eligible drivers until both quotas are filled.

  2. Stratified sampling selects randomly within each group; quota sampling selects available people non-randomly until the quotas are full.

  3. Quota sampling does not require a complete sampling frame and can be quicker to organise.

  4. An entering driver may be a visitor, and the car may be borrowed or hired rather than owned by that driver. The observations therefore do not reliably measure cars owned by residents.

solutions.method: Numerical measurements are quantitative; categories are qualitative.

steps.explanation: Height: quantitative, because it is a numerical measurement.
Hair colour: qualitative, because it is a category.
Running time: quantitative, because it is a numerical measurement.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Numerical measurements are quantitative; categories are qualitative.

  1. Height: quantitative, because it is a numerical measurement.

  2. Hair colour: qualitative, because it is a category.

  3. Running time: quantitative, because it is a numerical measurement.

solutions.method: Counts are discrete; measured dimensions can vary continuously.

steps.explanation: Worm length is continuous.
Number of slugs is discrete, taking whole-number values.
Ant height is continuous.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Counts are discrete; measured dimensions can vary continuously.

  1. Worm length is continuous.

  2. Number of slugs is discrete, taking whole-number values.

  3. Ant height is continuous.

solutions.method: Mass is measured on a continuous scale.

steps.explanation: Within the measurement range, mass can take any real value rather than only separate count values.

1. Boundaries: 45 kg and 50 kg.

  2. Class width: 50−45=5 kg.

  3. Midpoint: (45+50)/2=47.5 kg.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Mass is measured on a continuous scale.

  1. Within the measurement range, mass can take any real value rather than only separate count values.

    1. Boundaries: 45 kg and 50 kg.

    2. Class width: 50−45=5 kg.

    3. Midpoint: (45+50)/2=47.5 kg.

solutions.method: Distinguish a count of caterpillars from their measured lengths.

steps.explanation: Discrete: the number on a tree is a whole-number count.
Use four strata for trees with 7, 8, 9 and 10 caterpillars. Rounded allocations 8, 4, 6 and 2 total 20; select that many different trees randomly within each stratum.
The lengths are continuous quantitative data because length is measured rather than counted.

solutions.solutionHtml:

  2. Use four strata for trees with 7, 8, 9 and 10 caterpillars. Rounded allocations 8, 4, 6 and 2 total 20; select that many different trees randomly within each stratum.

  3. The lengths are continuous quantitative data because length is measured rather than counted.

solutions.method: Compare the positions of the five UK large-data-set stations.

steps.explanation: Leuchars is furthest north.
Camborne is furthest south.
Camborne is furthest west.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Compare the positions of the five UK large-data-set stations.

  1. Leuchars is furthest north.

  2. Camborne is furthest south.

  3. Camborne is furthest west.

solutions.method: Specify the recorded daily quantity and unit.

steps.explanation: The total precipitation during the 24-hour period, including the water equivalent of snow or hail, measured in millimetres.
The highest gust speed recorded during the day, measured in knots.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Specify the recorded daily quantity and unit.

  1. The total precipitation during the 24-hour period, including the water equivalent of snow or hail, measured in millimetres.

  2. The highest gust speed recorded during the day, measured in knots.

solutions.method: A north–south investigation needs sufficient observations and a useful spread of latitude.

steps.explanation:
1. Five days is too small to establish a reliable pattern.

  2. Heathrow and Hurn have relatively similar latitudes; include more widely separated stations to investigate the effect of moving north.
Number all 184 dates in Heathrow’s 2015 data 1–184. Generate 15 distinct random integers, rejecting repeats, and select the corresponding dates.
A repeated date would not add a new sampling unit. Reject the duplicate and keep drawing random numbers until there are 15 different dates.

solutions.solutionHtml:
A north–south investigation needs sufficient observations and a useful spread of latitude.

    1. Five days is too small to establish a reliable pattern.

    2. Heathrow and Hurn have relatively similar latitudes; include more widely separated stations to investigate the effect of moving north.

  2. Number all 184 dates in Heathrow’s 2015 data 1–184. Generate 15 distinct random integers, rejecting repeats, and select the corresponding dates.

  3. A repeated date would not add a new sampling unit. Reject the duplicate and keep drawing random numbers until there are 15 different dates.

solutions.method: Latitude and sample size both affect the comparison.

steps.explanation: Leuchars is farther north than Camborne, so lower mean temperatures are plausible.
Five days per location is a small sample. Use more dates, preferably the same dates at both stations, so the comparison is less affected by different sampled weather periods.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Latitude and sample size both affect the comparison.

  1. Leuchars is farther north than Camborne, so lower mean temperatures are plausible.

  2. Five days per location is a small sample. Use more dates, preferably the same dates at both stations, so the comparison is less affected by different sampled weather periods.

solutions.method: Keep genuine low-rainfall days in the sample.

steps.explanation: In the ordered list choose a random starting position from 1–9, then take that date and the next 19 dates nine positions apart. Stop after 20 observations. A fractional-interval systematic design using interval 9.2 is also possible.
“tr” means a trace of rainfall, less than 0.05 mm. Discarding these valid low-rainfall observations and replacing them biases the sample towards wetter days.
Retain the dates and treat trace values as 0 mm for the prescribed calculation, noting that this is a small-value approximation.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Keep genuine low-rainfall days in the sample.

  1. In the ordered list choose a random starting position from 1–9, then take that date and the next 19 dates nine positions apart. Stop after 20 observations. A fractional-interval systematic design using interval 9.2 is also possible.

  2. “tr” means a trace of rainfall, less than 0.05 mm. Discarding these valid low-rainfall observations and replacing them biases the sample towards wetter days.

  3. Retain the dates and treat trace values as 0 mm for the prescribed calculation, noting that this is a small-value approximation.

solutions.method: A maximum cannot lie below the mean of the same wind observations.

steps.explanation: The daily maximum gust cannot be below the daily mean windspeed; 25<31, so at least one reading is wrong.
11 knots lies in Beaufort force 4 (11–16 knots), described as a moderate breeze.

  2. 11 knots lies in Beaufort force 4 (11–16 knots), described as a moderate breeze.

solutions.method: Use seasonal and geographical contrasts, rather than identifying stations from windspeed alone.

steps.explanation: A is Hurn: a moderate northern-hemisphere summer temperature of 16.8°C.
B is Beijing: the hottest of these July averages, 26.8°C.
C is Perth: July is winter in Australia, consistent with the lowest average, 13.3°C.

solutions.method: Select distinct dates across the entire period.

steps.explanation: Number the 184 dates and generate five distinct random integers from 1–184; use the corresponding rainfall observations.
Advantage: every date has an equal chance of selection. Disadvantage: five randomly selected dates may not represent the weather across all the months.
Increase the sample size, retaining random selection across the full set of dates.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Select distinct dates across the entire period.

  1. Number the 184 dates and generate five distinct random integers from 1–184; use the corresponding rainfall observations.

  2. Advantage: every date has an equal chance of selection. Disadvantage: five randomly selected dates may not represent the weather across all the months.

  3. Increase the sample size, retaining random selection across the full set of dates.

solutions.method: Count how many dates the systematic interval actually reaches.

steps.explanation: Systematic sampling, because there is a random start followed by every fifth value.
Starting at 1 or 2 gives 19 dates; starting at 3, 4 or 5 gives 18. Neither gives the required 20.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Count how many dates the systematic interval actually reaches.

  1. Systematic sampling, because there is a random start followed by every fifth value.

  2. Starting at 1 or 2 gives 19 dates; starting at 3, 4 or 5 gives 18. Neither gives the required 20.

solutions.method: Allocate in proportion to month length, rounding to a total of 15.

steps.explanation: Choose five different dates at random from May, five from June and five from July.
Every month is represented, reducing the risk that the sample is concentrated in only one month.
Wind direction is recorded as a bearing in degrees and as a compass direction.

solutions.method: The first people encountered form a convenience sample.

steps.explanation: Opportunity sampling.
It is quick and easy to organise.
Ask more students and use a random or stratified selection from the year-group list instead of only the first people encountered.

solutions.solutionHtml:
The first people encountered form a convenience sample.

  1. Opportunity sampling.

  2. It is quick and easy to organise.

  3. Ask more students and use a random or stratified selection from the year-group list instead of only the first people encountered.

solutions.method: Systematic sampling needs a random start.

steps.explanation: Systematic sampling, provided its initial position is randomly selected.
Opportunity sampling is quick and inexpensive, but accessible students may not represent the school’s musical tastes.
Systematic sampling spreads selections through the list, but it needs a sampling frame and can be distorted by a repeating pattern in that list.
Use systematic sampling from the school register with a random start and suitable interval, checking the list has no periodic pattern. It gives broader coverage than asking only nearby students.

solutions.solutionHtml:
Systematic sampling needs a random start.

  1. Systematic sampling, provided its initial position is randomly selected.

  2. Opportunity sampling is quick and inexpensive, but accessible students may not represent the school’s musical tastes.

  3. Systematic sampling spreads selections through the list, but it needs a sampling frame and can be distorted by a repeating pattern in that list.

  4. Use systematic sampling from the school register with a random start and suitable interval, checking the list has no periodic pattern. It gives broader coverage than asking only nearby students.

solutions.method: Choose accessible shoppers, then set population-based quotas.

steps.explanation: A central market square is likely to contain many shoppers on a Saturday afternoon, making it practical to fill quotas. It may still omit people who shop at other times.
For example: men aged 18–39, women aged 18–39, men aged 40 or over, and women aged 40 or over. All groups consist only of adults.
Use suitable population statistics to estimate each group’s proportion, multiply those proportions by the planned sample size, and round allocations so their sum equals the sample size.

  3. Use suitable population statistics to estimate each group’s proportion, multiply those proportions by the planned sample size, and round allocations so their sum equals the sample size.

solutions.method: There are 160 pupils, and the desired sample fraction is one quarter.

steps.explanation: Number the year group 1–160. Choose r randomly from 1–4 and then take every fourth pupil, ending with r+156.
Randomly choose 19 distinct boys and 21 distinct girls from the respective lists.

solutions.method: Using the first available dates is not random selection.

steps.explanation: Opportunity sampling: the first five dates are chosen for convenience.

Simple random sampling: label all June dates and choose five distinct random dates; it is easy to perform, but a small sample may cluster in one part of June. Systematic sampling: choose a random start from 1–6 and then every sixth day; this spreads the sample across June, but periodic patterns or missing readings can cause problems.
Continuous: daily sunshine duration is measured and can take any value within its possible range, even if the recorded values are rounded.

  1. Opportunity sampling: the first five dates are chosen for convenience.

  2. Simple random sampling: label all June dates and choose five distinct random dates; it is easy to perform, but a small sample may cluster in one part of June. Systematic sampling: choose a random start from 1–6 and then every sixth day; this spreads the sample across June, but periodic patterns or missing readings can cause problems.

  3. Continuous: daily sunshine duration is measured and can take any value within its possible range, even if the recorded values are rounded.

solutions.method: Distinguish a sample mean from a guaranteed minimum.

steps.explanation: A census would burst every inner tube, destroying all the stock.
Although the mean exceeds 600 kPa, two of the five tubes burst below 600 kPa. A claim that every tube withstands at least 600 kPa is therefore contradicted by the sample.
Test a larger random sample, ideally across production batches.

solutions.method: A simple random sample contains distinct, equally likely units.

steps.explanation: A sampling unit is one individual item or member of the population.

Number the 184 dates 1–184 and generate 20 distinct random integers in that range, rejecting duplicates; use the windspeed on those dates.
Each date has a known equal chance of selection, avoiding deliberate selection bias; with an existing numbered list it is straightforward and inexpensive.
